If there's one sockeye in the river, it's on his line.

Some people fish. Lyndon has a system.

Lyndon works the Kenai like a craftsman works his shop. He watches the water, times the runs, and puts his line exactly where the sockeye are going to be. He's patient and methodical, and he's the best fisherman alive. Ask anyone who's stood next to him.

If you've fished with him, you've been coached. If you haven't heard the rules yet, here's your head start.

The Whisperer's Rules

Shouted from the bank. Obey them.

  1. Keep your rod tip up!Once he's hooked, keep that tip high and out of the water.

  2. Don't pull its head out of the water!Lift his head and he runs. Keep it under.

  3. Keep your net in the water and scoop it!Let him swim in close, then scoop.

Posted by order of the Sockeye Whisperer

Smoked Salmon Secrets

Lyndon's step-by-step method, from the riverbank to the smoker. Fresh fish, a simple dry brine, and patience.

  • The brineFour parts brown sugar to one part salt. No liquids.
  • The waitTwelve to sixteen hours in the fridge, turned halfway.
  • The chipsAlder or apple. Hickory and mesquite are too strong.
  • The smokeAbout 140°. Eight to twelve hours to serve, three to four to can.
“Some Alaskans use old, freezer-burned fish for smoking. I say, cook it for the dog!”

The Air Catch

A sockeye jumped, the hook popped loose, and the fish went airborne. Aubrey swung the net and caught it mid-air. He still tells that story.

The front has his netting rule. The back has the catch that broke it.
